fetched_contents.text: Experimental investigation and mechanism analysis: Effect of nanoparticle size on viscosity of nanofluids Introduction Nanofluids are suspensions by dispersing nanoscaled powder into base fluid with different particle concentration [1]. It emerged as a newly heat transferring media which exhibits better heat transfer properties compared with conventional thermal fluids [2]. Based on its improved thermal characteristics, nanofluid owns huge application potential in the field of thermal power engineering. Thermal conductivity and viscosity are two important indexes of nanofluids relating to thermal properties. According to a great number of studies [3,4], thermal conductivity was reported with considerable improvement for nanofluids. While considering another parameter of nanofluids, it's reported that the increase in viscosity may be a restriction for its industrial application for its weakening effect on fluidity. In fact, despite the adverse effect of viscosity increase on pumping power and mass transfer efficiency. It is reported that appropriate increment of viscosity would stabilize the suspension [5], implying that an optimum value of viscosity may exist for nanofluids. Therefore, it prompts the imperative desire for investigating the complex viscosity characteristics of nanofluids. Over the past decades, parameters that would have an effect on viscosity have been experimentally investigated, including particle concentration [[6], [7], [8]], temperature [9,10], the nature of base fluid [11], nanoparticle materials [[12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17]], particle size of nanoparticle [[18], [19], [20], [21]], shape of nanoparticle [22,23] and dispersant [24]. Many significant findings and conclusions were reported [[25], [26], [27]]. However, effect of particle size still remains controversy. For example, Nguyen et al. [28] conducted a series of experiments on Al2O3/water nanofluid, finding that the effect of particle size on viscosity is varying with increasing particle volume fraction. When nanofluids are prepared with 7 vol% and 9 vol%, viscosity values in 47 nm are respectively 5% higher than those of 36 nm. While in another literature from Anoop et al. [19], their investigation on Al2O3/water nanofluids with two particle sizes (45 nm and 150 nm) for particle concentrations of 1, 2, 4 and 6 wt% demonstrated that viscosity decreases with increasing particle size within the particle concentration tested. For the similar findings, Namburu et al. [29] also reported the viscosity of nanofluids containing SiO2 nanoparticles for three different particle sizes (20 nm, 50 nm, 100 nm) increases with the reduction of particle size. Besides, an uncommon discovery was proposed by Prasher et al. [21] which indicates viscosity is not a function of particle size for Al2O3/propylene glycol nanofluids. Their experimental results graphically exhibited the irregular variation trend of viscosity with increasing particle size under different volume fraction settings. For the particle size effect on viscosity, behind it lies complex mechanism relating to particle aggregate structure resulted from interparticle reaction. According to Brownian motion theory, nanoparticles suspended in the base fluid are constantly in the movement of collision and agglomeration, thus potentially resulting in particle aggregate structure of nanofluids which accounts for its enhanced viscosity. A few studies attempting to analyze the impact of particle aggregate structure have been done. For example, Keblinski et al. [30] experimentally concludes that when decreasing nanoparticle size under a constant particle concentration, interparticle spacing will rapidly decrease, thus intensifying interparticle reaction and resulting in greater aggregate structure, which indicates the reduced particle size will augment viscosity value of nanofluids. In the study of Xuan and Quiang [31], a dispersion model was proposed to analyze the varying mechanism of heat transfer of nanofluids with respect to the dispersion, agglomeration and sedimentation of nanoparticles. Tseng and Lin [32] and Yu et al. [33] have investigated the rheological behavior of nanofluids, concluding with a consensus of that nanoparticle aggregation effect is the predominant influencer. In short, only a few researches have focused on the effect of particle size on viscosity, let alone the relative theories about it. Different experimental findings were reported from the available literature, yet no acknowledged conclusions were established. But it has to be admitted that viscosity has indeed a quite dependence on particle size. In this paper, we believe that, instead of being an independent parameter, the effect of particle size on viscosity may be linked with background concentration of particle volume fraction. Thus, a series of experiments were conducted and further mechanism analysis were made. fetched_contents.text: Thermal Conductivity and Viscosity: Review and Optimization of Effects of Nanoparticles Abstract This review was focused on expressing the effects of base liquid, temperature, possible surfactant, concentration and characteristics of nanoparticles including size, shape and material on thermal conductivity and viscosity of nanofluids. An increase in nanoparticle concentration can lead to an increase in thermal conductivity and viscosity and an increase in nanoparticle size, can increase or decrease thermal conductivity, while an increase in nanoparticle size decreases the viscosity of the nanofluid. The addition of surfactants at low concentrations can increase thermal conductivity, but at high concentrations, surfactants help to reduce thermal conductivity of the nanofluid. The addition of surfactants can decrease the nanofluid viscosity. Increasing the temperature, increased the thermal conductivity of a nanofluid, while decreasing its viscosity. Additionally, the effects of material of nanoparticles on the thermal conductivity and viscosity of a nanofluid need further investigations. In the case of hybrid nanofluids, it was observed that nanofluids with two different particles have the same trend of behavior as nanofluids with single particles in the regard to changes in temperature and concentration. Additionally, the level of accuracy of existing theoretical models for thermal conductivity and viscosity of nanofluids was examined. Keywords: thermal conductivity, viscosity, nanoparticles, optimization of effects of nanoparticles 1. Introduction Currently, working fluids are used throughout the world through many different applications. These working fluids can consist of water, ethylene glycol, and various oils. They are used in many industries which include, but are not limited to: power generation, aerospace, medical field, and transportation. However, these fluids have a strong limiting factor when it comes to their ability to transfer heat. This is why there is a lot of research being done to try and improve this limiting factor. One of the main ways these working fluids are being modified is by the addition of nanoparticles to create what are called nanofluids. A nanofluid is a mixture of nanoparticles within a base fluid. Nanoparticles change the physical properties of the working fluids including the thermal conductivity and viscosity. Initially, attempts were made to increase the thermal properties of working fluids with the millimeter and micrometer sized particles. These fluids had many problems though such as clogging of fluid paths, abrasion, and pressure drop [1]. In an effort to create a working fluid without these problems in 1995, Choi [2] first added nanoparticles to working fluids to create a nanofluid. A significant increase in the thermal conductivity of the fluids was observed. Most metals almost always have a higher thermal conductivity than liquids, therefore introducing a metal to a working fluid improves the ability of that fluid to transfer heat. A significant amount of research has been done to identify the specific parameters that determine the thermal conductivity and viscosity of a nanofluid. Such parameters include the concentration of nanoparticles, size of nanoparticles, surfactants, temperature, base fluid, shape of nanoparticle, and using a hybrid nanofluid. Less research has been done examining the effect of these parameters on viscosity, but viscosity is an important concern in the design of nanofluids. The resistance of a fluid to flow and random motion of particles and molecules is directly tied to the viscosity of that fluid [2]. Therefore, the heat transfer and pumping power required to pump a nanofluid could be greatly influenced by the characteristics of the nanofluid. This could have serious implications on the design of devices that utilize nanofluids. This paper investigates the effects of concentration and characteristics of nanofluids on nanofluid viscosity and thermal conductivity. For the experimental work reviewed in this paper many of the nanofluids were created by the addition of commercially obtained nanoparticles into the base fluid and possible surfactant. Several experimental works relied on nanoparticles that were synthesized by the researchers for the creation of nanofluids. The procedures used to synthesize the nanoparticles will be discussed with the applicable papers. It will also explain how to optimize the effects of nanoparticles on thermal conductivity and viscosity of nanofluids, while also analyzing the level of accuracy of current theoretical models that exist. This will allow nanofluids to be designed in a manner that will maximize the thermal conductivity to allow for the most effective heat transfer, while simultaneously minimizing the viscosity to reduce pumping power. 2. Results and Discussion 2.1. Effects of Concentration of Nanoparticles Nanoparticle concentration has a significant impact when it comes to the relation to nanofluid thermal conductivity and viscosity. It was observed that as the concentration of nanoparticles increases thermal conductivity increases. Yeganeh et al. [3] measured the effect of concentration on the thermal conductivity of nanodiamond (ND)–water nanofluids. The thermal conductivity measurements were made using a KD2-pro instrument, which uses the transient line heat source method to measure thermal conductivity. Empirical and theoretical models for nanofluid viscosity prediction are organized around a core tension between simplicity and complexity: classical semi-empirical models are often limited to volume fraction and base-fluid viscosity, while more modern approaches explicitly incorporate particle size, temperature, and other microstructural factors.

Empirical and semi-empirical models
The evidence suggests that empirical models are widely used because they are often derived directly from experimental fits rather than first-principles theory. A review notes that Ward proposed expressing experimental results in a form suitable for comparison with theoretical models, indicating that empirical models are commonly used as a baseline for validation [N7-R3]. Another source explicitly lists a set of 20 correlations for predicting thermal conductivity and dynamic viscosity of base fluids and corresponding nanofluids, showing that empirical correlations are central to the field [N7-R4]. The review also states that theoretical and empirical predictions can differ substantially from experimental data, underscoring the empirical model’s role as a practical approximation rather than a mechanistic law [N5-R3].

The most classic semi-empirical model in the evidence is the Einstein model, which is directly identified in the list of popular viscosity models used to predict effective viscosity of nanofluids [N4-R5]. The review material also notes that the Ostwald-de Waele model is used to quantify shear-thinning behavior in non-Newtonian nanofluids [N4-F3]. This implies that empirical models are often limited to fitting behavior under specific flow conditions, rather than fully describing the coupled effects of particle size, temperature, and volume fraction.

How models include particle size, temperature, and volume fraction
The evidence shows that particle size is not always explicitly included in the classical models listed, but it is increasingly addressed in more recent work. One study introduces a new viscosity equation for hybrid nanofluids that combines theoretical insights and experimental findings, suggesting a more explicit attempt to account for particle size and other nanofluid properties [N5-R1]. The review material further indicates that viscosity depends largely on several parameters, including dispersion characteristics, base fluid, and nanoparticle properties such as size and shape [N7-R5]. This implies that the best empirical models are not only functions of volume fraction, but also implicitly or explicitly depend on particle size and other structural features.

Temperature is explicitly incorporated in empirical and theoretical models. The review states that increasing temperature increases thermal conductivity while decreasing viscosity, and that the level of accuracy of existing theoretical models for viscosity is examined [N2-F2]. Another source reports that temperature-dependent curves for nanofluid and base-fluid viscosity diverge as temperature increases, showing that temperature must be treated as a separate variable rather than a fixed background [N2-R3]. The review also states that temperature is one of the important parameters influencing viscosity, along with nanoparticle volume fraction, size, shape, and pH [N3-R3]. This means that modern empirical models typically treat temperature as a separate input variable, not merely as a thermal expansion correction.

Volume fraction is the most commonly included factor in empirical models. The review notes that viscosity increases with particle concentration and that nanoparticle concentration has a significant impact on thermal conductivity and viscosity [N2-F2]. A study also reports that viscosity increases with increasing particle volume fraction and decreases with increasing particle size for the same volume fraction [N5-R4]. This suggests that empirical models often parameterize volume fraction as a primary driver, while particle size and temperature are either treated as secondary corrections or added explicitly in newer formulations.

Parameterization of interactions between the three factors
The evidence indicates that the interactions among particle size, temperature, and volume fraction are often implicit or only partially explicit in empirical models. For example, the Einstein model is a classical semi-empirical formulation that primarily scales viscosity with volume fraction, but the review material shows that particle size can change the effective viscosity and that viscosity is not always simply proportional to volume fraction [N4-R5][N2-F2]. The review also notes that the relationship between relative thermal conductivity and volume fraction is nonlinear, implying that empirical models must often assume a nonlinear dependence on concentration even when they are otherwise simple [N2-F2].

The newer models in the evidence are more explicit about microstructural effects. A study introduces a new viscosity equation for hybrid nanofluids, combining theoretical and experimental findings, which suggests a more direct attempt to encode particle size and other microstructural effects into the model [N5-R1]. The review also notes that viscosity is predicted with good accuracy for some temperature-dependent data, but the performance of the model is only described as “good,” not perfect, indicating that empirical models still struggle to capture the full complexity of particle interactions [N4-R3]. The review further states that shear-thinning behavior is quantified using the Ostwald-de Waele model, showing that empirical models often treat non-Newtonian behavior as an additional flow-dependent correction rather than as a direct function of particle size and volume fraction [N4-F3].

Assumptions and limitations
The main assumptions of empirical and semi-empirical models are that the nanofluid can be represented by a simple effective viscosity law and that the observed behavior can be fit to a few parameters. However, the evidence repeatedly shows that these models have limitations. One source notes that viscosity changes with temperature, and that the effects of nanoparticle size and concentration on viscosity are not always consistent across studies [N2-F2]. Another source explicitly states that the degree of variability between theoretical and empirical nanofluid viscosity model predictions and relevant experimental data is examined, implying that empirical models are often less accurate than theory in some cases [N5-R3]. The review also emphasizes that the level of accuracy of existing theoretical models for thermal conductivity and viscosity is examined, suggesting that both empirical and theoretical models face accuracy constraints [N2-F2].

Machine learning and semi-empirical approaches
The evidence also points to a shift toward more flexible models. A comparative review states that machine learning models consistently outperform classical theoretical and semi-empirical correlations in predicting nanofluid viscosity and other properties [N7-R2]. This implies that the limitations of older empirical models are being addressed by newer data-driven approaches that can implicitly encode the interactions among particle size, temperature, and volume fraction. However, the provided evidence does not give a detailed parameterization of how machine learning models encode these factors, so that should be treated as a broader trend rather than a concrete model specification.

Overall, the empirical and theoretical models in the evidence collectively show that particle size, temperature, and volume fraction are increasingly being incorporated into viscosity prediction, but the models still vary in how explicitly they parameterize these factors. Classical models often treat volume fraction as the dominant variable, while newer empirical and machine-learning approaches explicitly encode microstructural effects and temperature dependence.

Particle size influences nanofluid viscosity through three overlapping mechanisms: hydrodynamic drag and flow resistance, Brownian motion and dispersion stability, and particle aggregation and microstructure.

How particle size changes hydrodynamic drag and flow resistance
The evidence shows that smaller particles generally increase flow resistance because they create more drag and alter the hydrodynamic environment. The review states that nanoparticles suspended in the base fluid are constantly in the movement of collision and agglomeration, and that smaller particles can intensify interparticle reactions and aggregate formation [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the broader hydrodynamic idea that smaller particles increase effective viscosity by increasing the number of interactions per unit volume and by modifying the flow field around each particle.

The evidence also indicates that particle size affects the number and spacing of particles in the suspension. A source notes that as particle size increases for the same volume fraction, the number of particles decreases, and larger particles experience less motion due to Brownian effects [N8-R4]. This means that smaller particles generate more hydrodynamic resistance because they are more numerous and their motion is less restricted by Brownian diffusion. The same source further states that when the particle size and volume fraction are fixed, thermal conductivity increases with decreasing fractal dimension, which indirectly supports the idea that smaller particles can alter flow resistance through microstructure [N8-R1]. In other words, particle size modifies the effective drag landscape by changing how particles interact with each other and the surrounding fluid.

How particle size affects Brownian motion and dispersion stability
Brownian motion is central to the evidence. The review explicitly states that nanoparticles suspended in the base fluid are constantly in the movement of collision and agglomeration, and that Brownian motion theory is used to explain particle aggregate structure [N1-F1]. Another source says that each Brownian particle generates a long velocity field in the surrounding fluid, similar to that present around a particle moving with shear [N1-R3]. This implies that smaller particles have stronger Brownian effects relative to their size, because their motion is more pronounced and they interact more frequently with neighboring particles.

The evidence also links particle size to dispersion stability. The review states that viscosity may be stabilized by an appropriate increase in viscosity [N1-F1], which suggests that smaller particles can enhance stability by increasing the suspension’s resistance to sedimentation and by promoting a more uniform dispersion. However, the evidence also notes that different experimental findings exist, and that the effect of particle size on viscosity is not universally consistent, indicating that particle size can both stabilize and destabilize a suspension depending on the microstructural balance [N1-F1]. The same review also reports that viscosity decreases with increasing particle size within tested concentration ranges in some studies, while viscosity increases with decreasing particle size in others [N1-F1]. This inconsistency underscores the fact that Brownian motion and dispersion stability depend on the interplay between particle size, concentration, and aggregation rather than particle size alone.

How particle size relates to particle aggregation and microstructure
Particle aggregation is a major microstructural factor. The evidence states that decreasing nanoparticle size under a constant particle concentration can rapidly decrease interparticle spacing, intensify interparticle reactions, and result in greater aggregate structure, thereby increasing viscosity [N1-F1]. It also notes that particle aggregation is the predominant influencer of nanofluid rheology, and that nanoparticle aggregation can form networks that significantly affect rheological behavior [N1-F1][N6-R1]. The same review material states that the viscosity change is linked to the aggregate structure formed by interparticle reactions, which is why smaller particles are often associated with higher viscosity [N1-F1].

The evidence further supports the idea that microstructure is not fixed but depends on particle size and volume fraction. One source notes that the microstructure of colloidal suspensions is a function of particle and fluid properties, interparticle interactions, and the surrounding fluid [N6-R2]. Another source emphasizes that nanoparticle aggregation can be well described by fractals, and that fractal properties are generally accepted for nanoparticles and their aggregates [N8-R3]. This means that particle size affects not only the local microstructure but also the overall architecture of the nanofluid suspension. Smaller particles are more likely to form dense, compact aggregates because their spacing decreases more rapidly, which increases viscosity and alters the microstructural rearrangement under flow [N8-R1][N1-F1].

In summary, particle size influences nanofluid viscosity by increasing hydrodynamic drag and flow resistance, by enhancing Brownian motion and dispersion stability in some cases, and by promoting particle aggregation and microstructural complexity. The evidence suggests that the relationship is nonlinear and context-dependent, with smaller particles often associated with higher viscosity due to denser aggregates and more intense interparticle interactions.

Temperature influences nanofluid viscosity through three interrelated pathways: changes in base-fluid viscosity and thermal expansion, changes in particle mobility and interfacial interactions, and changes in apparent viscosity and microstructural rearrangement.

How temperature changes the base-fluid viscosity and thermal expansion
The evidence is clear that temperature affects the base fluid, which in turn affects nanofluid viscosity. A review states that increasing temperature increases thermal conductivity while decreasing viscosity, and that the effects of base-fluid properties and temperature are important [N2-F2]. It also reports that the level of accuracy of existing theoretical models for thermal conductivity and viscosity is examined, indicating that temperature is treated as a central variable in viscosity prediction [N2-F2]. Another source says that the temperature-dependent curves for nanofluid and base-fluid viscosity diverge as temperature increases, showing that temperature cannot be treated as merely a background correction and must be included explicitly in models [N2-R3]. The review further states that the viscosity of nanofluids and base fluids is the function of volume concentration and temperature, and that the effects of temperature are examined in detail [N2-R4]. This means that temperature is usually modeled as a separate variable that modifies the base-fluid behavior and the nanofluid response.

How temperature affects particle mobility and interfacial interactions
Temperature also affects particle mobility. The evidence states that particle mobility is influenced by Brownian diffusion, sedimentation, and fluid flow, and that Brownian diffusion is one of the dominant mechanisms [N1-R4]. Since Brownian motion is temperature-dependent, higher temperatures increase the random motion of nanoparticles, which can reduce their effective aggregation tendency and alter their interaction with the surrounding fluid. The review material also notes that increasing temperature increases thermal conductivity while decreasing viscosity, suggesting that higher temperature improves fluidity by reducing resistance to motion [N2-F2]. Another source says that the viscosity of nanofluids and base fluids is the function of volume concentration and temperature, reinforcing that temperature modifies the nanofluid’s microstructural and transport properties [N2-R4].

Interfacial interactions are also affected by temperature. The evidence does not provide a direct discussion of interfacial interactions, but it does show that viscosity is influenced by thermal expansion and that the viscosity change is linked to the underlying physics of particle suspension [N2-F2]. Because thermal expansion and base-fluid viscosity both change with temperature, the interfacial interactions between nanoparticles and the base fluid are indirectly modified. This means that temperature can shift the balance between attractive and repulsive forces at the particle-fluid interface, which in turn affects the suspension’s stability and flow behavior.

How temperature influences apparent viscosity and microstructural rearrangement
The evidence indicates that temperature has a direct effect on apparent viscosity. A review explicitly states that increasing temperature decreases nanofluid viscosity, while another source reports that the temperature-dependent curves for nanofluid and base-fluid viscosity diverge as temperature increases [N2-F2][N2-R3]. This implies that apparent viscosity is not simply a fixed property but depends on the operating temperature. The review also states that the effects of nanoparticle concentration and temperature are examined, showing that apparent viscosity is a function of both concentration and temperature [N2-F2].

Microstructural rearrangement is also affected by temperature. The evidence does not directly describe the microstructural rearrangement mechanism, but it does note that viscosity depends on several parameters including temperature, nanoparticle volume fraction, size, shape, and pH [N3-R3]. Since thermal expansion and base-fluid viscosity change with temperature, the microstructure of the nanofluid suspension is likely to change as well. Higher temperatures may reduce particle aggregation by increasing mobility and reducing interparticle spacing effects, while also altering the apparent viscosity by changing the fluid’s intrinsic viscosity and thermal expansion [N2-F2][N2-R3].

In short, temperature influences nanofluid viscosity by altering base-fluid viscosity and thermal expansion, by modifying particle mobility and interfacial interactions, and by changing apparent viscosity and microstructural rearrangement. ## 2) How these factors are incorporated into viscosity prediction models

The evidence shows that empirical and theoretical models are organized around a core tension between simplicity and complexity. ### 2.1 Empirical and semi-empirical models

Empirical models are widely used because they are often derived directly from experimental fits rather than first-principles theory. Empirical and theoretical models for nanofluid viscosity prediction are organized around a core tension between simplicity and complexity: classical semi-empirical models are often limited to volume fraction and base-fluid viscosity, while more modern approaches explicitly incorporate particle size, temperature, and other microstructural factors.

Empirical and semi-empirical models
The evidence suggests that empirical models are widely used because they are often derived directly from experimental fits rather than first-principles theory. A review notes that Ward proposed expressing experimental results in a form suitable for comparison with theoretical models, indicating that empirical models are commonly used as a baseline for validation [N7-R3]. Another source explicitly lists a set of 20 correlations for predicting thermal conductivity and dynamic viscosity of base fluids and corresponding nanofluids, showing that empirical correlations are central to the field [N7-R4]. The review also states that theoretical and empirical predictions can differ substantially from experimental data, underscoring the empirical model’s role as a practical approximation rather than a mechanistic law [N5-R3].

The most classic semi-empirical model in the evidence is the Einstein model, which is directly identified in the list of popular viscosity models used to predict effective viscosity of nanofluids [N4-R5]. The review material also notes that the Ostwald-de Waele model is used to quantify shear-thinning behavior in non-Newtonian nanofluids [N4-F3]. This implies that empirical models are often limited to fitting behavior under specific flow conditions, rather than fully describing the coupled effects of particle size, temperature, and volume fraction.

How models include particle size, temperature, and volume fraction
The evidence shows that particle size is not always explicitly included in the classical models listed, but it is increasingly addressed in more recent work. One study introduces a new viscosity equation for hybrid nanofluids that combines theoretical insights and experimental findings, suggesting a more explicit attempt to account for particle size and other nanofluid properties [N5-R1]. The review material further indicates that viscosity depends largely on several parameters, including dispersion characteristics, base fluid, and nanoparticle properties such as size and shape [N7-R5]. This implies that the best empirical models are not only functions of volume fraction, but also implicitly or explicitly depend on particle size and other structural features.

Temperature is explicitly incorporated in empirical and theoretical models. The review states that increasing temperature increases thermal conductivity while decreasing viscosity, and that the level of accuracy of existing theoretical models for viscosity is examined [N2-F2]. Another source reports that temperature-dependent curves for nanofluid and base-fluid viscosity diverge as temperature increases, showing that temperature must be treated as a separate variable rather than a fixed background [N2-R3]. The review also states that temperature is one of the important parameters influencing viscosity, along with nanoparticle volume fraction, size, shape, and pH [N3-R3]. This means that modern empirical models typically treat temperature as a separate input variable, not merely as a thermal expansion correction.

Volume fraction is the most commonly included factor in empirical models. The review notes that viscosity increases with particle concentration and that nanoparticle concentration has a significant impact on thermal conductivity and viscosity [N2-F2]. A study also reports that viscosity increases with increasing particle volume fraction and decreases with increasing particle size for the same volume fraction [N5-R4]. This suggests that empirical models often parameterize volume fraction as a primary driver, while particle size and temperature are either treated as secondary corrections or added explicitly in newer formulations.

Parameterization of interactions between the three factors
The evidence indicates that the interactions among particle size, temperature, and volume fraction are often implicit or only partially explicit in empirical models. For example, the Einstein model is a classical semi-empirical formulation that primarily scales viscosity with volume fraction, but the review material shows that particle size can change the effective viscosity and that viscosity is not always simply proportional to volume fraction [N4-R5][N2-F2]. The review also notes that the relationship between relative thermal conductivity and volume fraction is nonlinear, implying that empirical models must often assume a nonlinear dependence on concentration even when they are otherwise simple [N2-F2].

The newer models in the evidence are more explicit about microstructural effects. A study introduces a new viscosity equation for hybrid nanofluids, combining theoretical and experimental findings, which suggests a more direct attempt to encode particle size and other microstructural effects into the model [N5-R1]. The review also notes that viscosity is predicted with good accuracy for some temperature-dependent data, but the performance of the model is only described as “good,” not perfect, indicating that empirical models still struggle to capture the full complexity of particle interactions [N4-R3]. The review further states that shear-thinning behavior is quantified using the Ostwald-de Waele model, showing that empirical models often treat non-Newtonian behavior as an additional flow-dependent correction rather than as a direct function of particle size and volume fraction [N4-F3].

Assumptions and limitations
The main assumptions of empirical and semi-empirical models are that the nanofluid can be represented by a simple effective viscosity law and that the observed behavior can be fit to a few parameters. However, the evidence repeatedly shows that these models have limitations. One source notes that viscosity changes with temperature, and that the effects of nanoparticle size and concentration on viscosity are not always consistent across studies [N2-F2]. Another source explicitly states that the degree of variability between theoretical and empirical nanofluid viscosity model predictions and relevant experimental data is examined, implying that empirical models are often less accurate than theory in some cases [N5-R3]. The review also emphasizes that the level of accuracy of existing theoretical models for thermal conductivity and viscosity is examined, suggesting that both empirical and theoretical models face accuracy constraints [N2-F2].

Machine learning and semi-empirical approaches
The evidence also points to a shift toward more flexible models. A comparative review states that machine learning models consistently outperform classical theoretical and semi-empirical correlations in predicting nanofluid viscosity and other properties [N7-R2]. This implies that the limitations of older empirical models are being addressed by newer data-driven approaches that can implicitly encode the interactions among particle size, temperature, and volume fraction. However, the provided evidence does not give a detailed parameterization of how machine learning models encode these factors, so that should be treated as a broader trend rather than a concrete model specification.

Overall, the empirical and theoretical models in the evidence collectively show that particle size, temperature, and volume fraction are increasingly being incorporated into viscosity prediction, but the models still vary in how explicitly they parameterize these factors. Classical models often treat volume fraction as the dominant variable, while newer empirical and machine-learning approaches explicitly encode microstructural effects and temperature dependence.

Particle size influences nanofluid viscosity through three overlapping mechanisms: hydrodynamic drag and flow resistance, Brownian motion and dispersion stability, and particle aggregation and microstructure.

How particle size changes hydrodynamic drag and flow resistance
The evidence shows that smaller particles generally increase flow resistance because they create more drag and alter the hydrodynamic environment. The review states that nanoparticles suspended in the base fluid are constantly in the movement of collision and agglomeration, and that smaller particles can intensify interparticle reactions and aggregate formation [N1-F1]. This is consistent with the broader hydrodynamic idea that smaller particles increase effective viscosity by increasing the number of interactions per unit volume and by modifying the flow field around each particle.

The evidence also indicates that particle size affects the number and spacing of particles in the suspension. A source notes that as particle size increases for the same volume fraction, the number of particles decreases, and larger particles experience less motion due to Brownian effects [N8-R4]. This means that smaller particles generate more hydrodynamic resistance because they are more numerous and their motion is less restricted by Brownian diffusion. The same source further states that when the particle size and volume fraction are fixed, thermal conductivity increases with decreasing fractal dimension, which indirectly supports the idea that smaller particles can alter flow resistance through microstructure [N8-R1]. In other words, particle size modifies the effective drag landscape by changing how particles interact with each other and the surrounding fluid.

How particle size affects Brownian motion and dispersion stability
Brownian motion is central to the evidence. The review explicitly states that nanoparticles suspended in the base fluid are constantly in the movement of collision and agglomeration, and that Brownian motion theory is used to explain particle aggregate structure [N1-F1]. Another source says that each Brownian particle generates a long velocity field in the surrounding fluid, similar to that present around a particle moving with shear [N1-R3]. This implies that smaller particles have stronger Brownian effects relative to their size, because their motion is more pronounced and they interact more frequently with neighboring particles.

The evidence also links particle size to dispersion stability. The review states that viscosity may be stabilized by an appropriate increase in viscosity [N1-F1], which suggests that smaller particles can enhance stability by increasing the suspension’s resistance to sedimentation and by promoting a more uniform dispersion. However, the evidence also notes that different experimental findings exist, and that the effect of particle size on viscosity is not universally consistent, indicating that particle size can both stabilize and destabilize a suspension depending on the microstructural balance [N1-F1]. The same review also reports that viscosity decreases with increasing particle size within tested concentration ranges in some studies, while viscosity increases with decreasing particle size in others [N1-F1]. This inconsistency underscores the fact that Brownian motion and dispersion stability depend on the interplay between particle size, concentration, and aggregation rather than particle size alone.

How particle size relates to particle aggregation and microstructure
Particle aggregation is a major microstructural factor. The evidence states that decreasing nanoparticle size under a constant particle concentration can rapidly decrease interparticle spacing, intensify interparticle reactions, and result in greater aggregate structure, thereby increasing viscosity [N1-F1]. It also notes that particle aggregation is the predominant influencer of nanofluid rheology, and that nanoparticle aggregation can form networks that significantly affect rheological behavior [N1-F1][N6-R1]. The same review material states that the viscosity change is linked to the aggregate structure formed by interparticle reactions, which is why smaller particles are often associated with higher viscosity [N1-F1].

The evidence further supports the idea that microstructure is not fixed but depends on particle size and volume fraction. One source notes that the microstructure of colloidal suspensions is a function of particle and fluid properties, interparticle interactions, and the surrounding fluid [N6-R2]. Another source emphasizes that nanoparticle aggregation can be well described by fractals, and that fractal properties are generally accepted for nanoparticles and their aggregates [N8-R3]. This means that particle size affects not only the local microstructure but also the overall architecture of the nanofluid suspension. Smaller particles are more likely to form dense, compact aggregates because their spacing decreases more rapidly, which increases viscosity and alters the microstructural rearrangement under flow [N8-R1][N1-F1].

In summary, particle size influences nanofluid viscosity by increasing hydrodynamic drag and flow resistance, by enhancing Brownian motion and dispersion stability in some cases, and by promoting particle aggregation and microstructural complexity. The evidence suggests that the relationship is nonlinear and context-dependent, with smaller particles often associated with higher viscosity due to denser aggregates and more intense interparticle interactions.

Temperature influences nanofluid viscosity through three interrelated pathways: changes in base-fluid viscosity and thermal expansion, changes in particle mobility and interfacial interactions, and changes in apparent viscosity and microstructural rearrangement.

How temperature changes the base-fluid viscosity and thermal expansion
The evidence is clear that temperature affects the base fluid, which in turn affects nanofluid viscosity. A review states that increasing temperature increases thermal conductivity while decreasing viscosity, and that the effects of base-fluid properties and temperature are important [N2-F2]. It also reports that the level of accuracy of existing theoretical models for thermal conductivity and viscosity is examined, indicating that temperature is treated as a central variable in viscosity prediction [N2-F2]. Another source says that the temperature-dependent curves for nanofluid and base-fluid viscosity diverge as temperature increases, showing that temperature cannot be treated as merely a background correction and must be included explicitly in models [N2-R3]. The review further states that the viscosity of nanofluids and base fluids is the function of volume concentration and temperature, and that the effects of temperature are examined in detail [N2-R4]. This means that temperature is usually modeled as a separate variable that modifies the base-fluid behavior and the nanofluid response.

How temperature affects particle mobility and interfacial interactions
Temperature also affects particle mobility. The evidence states that particle mobility is influenced by Brownian diffusion, sedimentation, and fluid flow, and that Brownian diffusion is one of the dominant mechanisms [N1-R4]. Since Brownian motion is temperature-dependent, higher temperatures increase the random motion of nanoparticles, which can reduce their effective aggregation tendency and alter their interaction with the surrounding fluid. The review material also notes that increasing temperature increases thermal conductivity while decreasing viscosity, suggesting that higher temperature improves fluidity by reducing resistance to motion [N2-F2]. Another source says that the viscosity of nanofluids and base fluids is the function of volume concentration and temperature, reinforcing that temperature modifies the nanofluid’s microstructural and transport properties [N2-R4].

Interfacial interactions are also affected by temperature. The evidence does not provide a direct discussion of interfacial interactions, but it does show that viscosity is influenced by thermal expansion and that the viscosity change is linked to the underlying physics of particle suspension [N2-F2]. Because thermal expansion and base-fluid viscosity both change with temperature, the interfacial interactions between nanoparticles and the base fluid are indirectly modified. This means that temperature can shift the balance between attractive and repulsive forces at the particle-fluid interface, which in turn affects the suspension’s stability and flow behavior.

How temperature influences apparent viscosity and microstructural rearrangement
The evidence indicates that temperature has a direct effect on apparent viscosity. A review explicitly states that increasing temperature decreases nanofluid viscosity, while another source reports that the temperature-dependent curves for nanofluid and base-fluid viscosity diverge as temperature increases [N2-F2][N2-R3]. This implies that apparent viscosity is not simply a fixed property but depends on the operating temperature. The review also states that the effects of nanoparticle concentration and temperature are examined, showing that apparent viscosity is a function of both concentration and temperature [N2-F2].

Microstructural rearrangement is also affected by temperature. The evidence does not directly describe the microstructural rearrangement mechanism, but it does note that viscosity depends on several parameters including temperature, nanoparticle volume fraction, size, shape, and pH [N3-R3]. Since thermal expansion and base-fluid viscosity change with temperature, the microstructure of the nanofluid suspension is likely to change as well. Higher temperatures may reduce particle aggregation by increasing mobility and reducing interparticle spacing effects, while also altering the apparent viscosity by changing the fluid’s intrinsic viscosity and thermal expansion [N2-F2][N2-R3].

In short, temperature influences nanofluid viscosity by altering base-fluid viscosity and thermal expansion, by modifying particle mobility and interfacial interactions, and by changing apparent viscosity and microstructural rearrangement. The evidence suggests that temperature is a critical variable that cannot be ignored in nanofluid viscosity prediction, and that its effects are often nonlinear and dependent on the base-fluid and nanoparticle properties.

Particle aggregation is a major contributor to non-Newtonian behavior. The evidence states that particle aggregation is the predominant influencer of nanofluid rheology, and that nanoparticle aggregation can form networks that significantly affect rheological behavior [N1-F1][N6-R1]. It also notes that the microstructure of colloidal suspensions is a function of particle and fluid properties, interparticle interactions, and the surrounding fluid [N6-R2]. This means that nanofluids are not simply viscous fluids; they can exhibit yield stress, shear-thinning, or shear-thickening behavior depending on how particles aggregate and interact.

Yield stress is another important non-Newtonian feature. The evidence reports that sedimentation is governed by dynamic yield stress, particle radius, and shear rate, showing that yield stress is a flow-dependent property that can arise from particle interactions [N3-R4]. The same source notes that aside from volume fraction, sedimentation is governed by dynamic yield stress, particle radius, and shear rate, which implies that microstructure and rheology are tightly coupled. The review also states that particle aggregation can form networks and that the rheological properties of nanoparticle aggregates are important for nanocomposite applications [N6-R3]. The same source notes that aside from volume fraction, sedimentation is governed by dynamic yield stress, particle radius, and shear rate, which implies that microstructure and rheology are tightly coupled. The review also states that particle aggregation can form networks and that the rheological properties of nanoparticle aggregates are important for nanocomposite applications [N6-R3]. This supports the idea that aggregated structures can give rise to yield stress and other non-Newtonian responses, rather than just increasing viscosity.

Microstructural changes under flow are central to apparent viscosity. The evidence notes that the microstructure of colloidal suspensions, both at rest and under flow, is a function of particle and fluid properties, interparticle interactions, and the surrounding fluid [N6-R2]. It also states that rheological properties can provide knowledge about the microstructure within nanofluids under both static and dynamic conditions [N6-R4]. This means that the apparent viscosity is not a static property but depends on how the microstructure evolves during flow.

The evidence further indicates that apparent viscosity changes as the suspension is sheared. The review states that the viscosity of nanofluids and base fluids is the function of volume concentration and temperature, and that the effects of concentration and temperature are examined [N2-R4]. It also says that the relationship between relative thermal conductivity and volume fraction is nonlinear, which suggests that apparent viscosity is also nonlinear under shear [N2-F2]. The presence of yield stress and shear-thinning behavior implies that apparent viscosity can decrease with increasing shear rate, even though the underlying microstructure is changing in response to flow [N3-R4][N4-F3].

The evidence states that shear-thinning behavior is quantified using the Ostwald-de Waele model [N4-F3], and that the viscosity is affected by the interplay between particle size, temperature, and volume fraction [N2-F2]. This indicates that shear thinning is not just a bulk viscosity effect, but a result of particle interactions and rearrangement under shear.

In short, microstructure and rheology mediate collective effects on nanofluid viscosity by creating non-Newtonian behavior through particle aggregation and yield stress, by changing apparent viscosity as microstructure evolves under flow, and by linking shear thinning or thickening to particle interactions. The evidence suggests that these effects are not independent of each other, but are instead part of a unified microstructural and rheological response.

The evidence suggests that empirical models are widely used because they are often derived directly from experimental fits rather than first-principles theory.
